passages.t: Now his eyes have seen God
passages.happening:
‘Then Job replied to the LORD’ (verse 1): “I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted” (verse 2).

He repeats God's own questions back to him, and answers them. “Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know” (verse 3).

“My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You. Therefore I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
These six verses are poetry, Job's last reply. He quotes God's words from 38:2-3 and 40:7 and answers them.

The hinge of the whole book is verse 5. Job had heard about God all his life. Now, after the whirlwind, he has seen him. The meeting has changed him, more than any answer to his question could have.

Dust and ashes is the rhyming pair Job used of himself in 30:19, the same words Abraham used before God.
passages.later: Abraham spoke of himself in the same words when he dared to plead with God: ‘though I am but dust and ashes’ (Genesis 18:27).
passages.hard:
What does Job take back, and what does he repent of?

The Hebrew of verse 6 is hard. The verb the BSB renders ‘retract’, maas, means to reject or despise, and in Hebrew it has no object. Translations supply one: he retracts his words, or despises himself, or rejects what he said. The verb rendered ‘repent’, nacham, can mean to be sorry or to change one's mind, but also to be comforted. So some scholars read the verse as Job being comforted concerning dust and ashes, finding consolation in his mortal state. The BSB's reading is the traditional one. The difficulty warns against building too much on any one translation.

Either way, Job's stance toward God has changed. What he does not do is confess the sins his friends charged him with. God never takes back his word that Job was blameless, and in the next verse he says that Job has spoken of him rightly. Job takes back his words spoken without knowledge, his claim to judge God's design. He does not take back his innocence.
passages.asks: Job had heard of God and then saw him. Ask whether your faith rests on what you have heard about God, or on meeting him. And ask what it would mean for you to let go of your demand for an answer, as Job did, without letting go of God.

passages.t: The friends rebuked, and Job prays for them
passages.happening:
After the LORD had spoken to Job, he said to Eliphaz: “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (verse 7).

They are to take seven bulls and seven rams, go to Job and offer a burnt offering for themselves. “Then My servant Job will pray for you, for I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly” (verse 8).

So Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar did as the LORD told them, ‘and the LORD accepted Job’s request’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The book returns to prose, and the epilogue mirrors the prologue in reverse. The friends who came to comfort Job are rebuked. The words ‘My servant Job’ (verse 8), first spoken in 1:8, come back four times in these verses.

The word for accurately, from kun, means what is right and firmly true. God says twice that the friends did not speak of him rightly, as Job did. Job's raw protests turned out to be more truthful about God than the friends' neat theology.

Seven bulls and seven rams were a large and costly offering, matching the seriousness of their fault. And the man they wrongly accused is the one who must pray for them. Eliphaz had promised that the returning sinner would pray for others and they would be rescued (22:30). It comes true, the other way round.

Elihu is not mentioned.
passages.asks: Job prayed for the friends who had wounded him. Ask whom you need to pray for, though they spoke wrongly to you in your pain. And ask whether you have spoken about God to a sufferer in a way that would need such a prayer.

passages.happening:
‘After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his prosperity and doubled his former possessions’ (verse 10). His brothers, sisters and old friends come and eat with him in his house, comfort him over all his trouble, and each gives him a piece of silver and a gold ring.

The LORD gives him 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen and 1,000 female donkeys. ‘And he also had seven sons and three daughters’ (verse 13). He names his daughters Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch. There are no women as beautiful as Job's daughters in all the land, ‘and their father granted them an inheritance among their brothers’ (verse 15).

Job lives 140 years and sees four generations. ‘And so Job died, old and full of years’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The phrase restored his prosperity, shevut, is the phrase later used of God restoring Israel after exile. The relatives who stayed away in Job's affliction (19:13-19) now come and eat with him, a full reconciliation. The piece of silver, a qesitah, is an old unit found otherwise only in the stories of Jacob and Joshua.

The numbers of animals are exactly twice those in 1:3. The children are given back in the same number, seven sons and three daughters.

The naming of the daughters is unusual. Biblical stories usually name sons and leave daughters unnamed, but here the daughters are named and the sons are not. Their names suggest beauty: Jemimah probably means dove, Keziah is the spice cassia, and Keren-happuch means horn of eye-paint. Job gives them an inheritance with their brothers, which went beyond Israel's later law, where daughters inherited only if there were no sons (Numbers 27:1-11).
passages.later: The New Testament remembers this ending: ‘You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy’ (James 5:11). And the last words of the book use the Hebrew phrase used of Abraham's death, which the BSB renders ‘old and contented’ (Genesis 25:8).
passages.hard:
Does the happy ending undo the book's message? And can new children replace the ones Job lost?

Many readers feel uneasy with the ending, and the feeling is honest. The book has argued at length that goodness and prosperity do not always go together, and then it ends by giving Job twice what he had. Some critics think the ending belonged to an older folk story that the poet kept without fully endorsing it. Others argue that it does not undo the message, because Job receives his restoration only after he has let go of his demand for it, and because it comes as a free gift, not a reward he could claim. The book as a whole says that God is free, not bound by a formula, and that includes his freedom to give.

The loss of Job's first children is not erased, and the text does not pretend otherwise. No new child replaces a lost one. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters have noted that Job's livestock was doubled while his children were given back only in the same number, and they have suggested that his first children were not lost forever but still counted as his. That reading is an inference the text does not state, and interpreters differ on it.

What the text does say is that Job lived to see four generations and died old and full of years, with grief behind him and good gifts around him. It does not promise that every sufferer's story will end in the same way in this life.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job's story ended in restoration, and his grief was still part of it. Ask whether you can hope for God's goodness without needing your story to end like Job's. And ask what it would mean to remember, as James does, that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
